A verse found in some manuscripts (the 'Gītāmāna') speaks of 745 verses (620 by Kṛṣṇa, 57 by Arjuna, 67 by Sañjaya, 1 by Dhṛtarāṣṭra); it is not in the Critical Edition.

attribution.scholarly: Usually dated c. 9th-10th c. CE and located in the Tamil south, in the milieu of the Āḻvārs; its style is deliberately archaic. Opponents of the text once alleged authorship by the 13th-c. grammarian Vopadeva (see dsp:which-bhagavata-is-the-mahapurana).

notes: Ācārakāṇḍa 1.142: the ten avatāras; 1.235-239 (approx.): brahma-jñāna, ātma-jñāna, Gītāsāra, Brahmagītāsāra; Pretakalpa 2.38.5: the seven liberating cities; Brahmakāṇḍa 3.1: its own sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa grading of the Purāṇas. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the Garuḍa Purāṇa (Venkateshwara ed.; Pretakalpa cited as 2.chapter.verse)
summary: A Vaiṣṇava encyclopedia best known for its Pretakalpa: the process of dying, Yama's messengers, the thumb-sized person, the year-long road to Yama's city past sixteen towns and the Vaitaraṇī river, judgment, the preta state and its signs, and the rites that give the dead a body and join them to the ancestors.

title: Garuḍa Purāṇa, Pretakalpa

attribution.tradition: Kṛṣṇa's answers to Garuḍa's questions on the fate of the dead (with a Bhīṣma-Yudhiṣṭhira dialogue in ch. 22).
attribution.scholarly: A manual of death and the rites for the dead; recensions differ in chapter count (35 in some editions).

structure.description: 49 chapters (Venkateshwara)

notes: Chapter topics (from the colophons of the local e-text): 1 questions; 2 after-death rites and karmic results; 3 hells; 4 cremation, deaths in pañcaka; 5 annual rites and the road to Yama; 6 vṛṣotsarga; 7 five pretas; 8 self-śrāddha; 11 the openings of departure; 12 only dharma follows the dead; 14 gifts; 15 Yama's world; 16 the preta's journey; 19 entry into Yama's hall and new bodies; 20-23 the abode, harassment, dreams and signs of pretas and their release; 24-25 untimely deaths and children; 26 sapiṇḍana; 27 Babhruvāhana and the preta; 32 embryology; 36 death by fasting; 38 higher worlds and liberation; 39 impurity periods; 44 bad deaths; 45 annual śrāddha; 46-48 destinies and karma; 49 means of liberation. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the Garuḍa Purāṇa (Venkateshwara ed.; Pretakalpa cited as 2.chapter.verse)
summary: The classical Purāṇic manual of dying and the afterlife: the signs and pains of death, the thumb-sized person led off by Yama's messengers, the airy conveyance-body and the body built by the ten days' piṇḍas, the year-long road, the Vaitaraṇī, judgment, the preta state and its release through the sons' rites, gifts to the dying, and the means of liberation.

title: Garuḍa Purāṇa Sāroddhāra

summary: A sixteen-chapter digest of the Garuḍa's teaching on death: the miseries of sinners, the road and city of Yama, the hells, rebirth and embryonic suffering, gifts and rites at death, the ten days, sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, and the conduct that leads to heaven or liberation.

Prefixed with Oṃ and the three vyāhṛtis (bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ) as in VS 36.3, it is the mantra given at initiation (upanayana) and repeated in the twilight worship; the tradition calls it the mother of the Vedas.

summary: The oldest extant complete commentary on the Gītā. summary: One of the three gems of the Pāñcarātra, in 33 paṭalas. Sages ask Śāṇḍilya, who relates Bhagavān's teaching to Nārada. Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 27 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Devavibhava (Kiraṇa: Devapitṛ), then the sage Saṃvartaka. The Kāmika assigns it 9 upabheda(s): Gāruḍa, Nairṛta, Nīla, Rūkṣa, Bhānuka, Dhenuka, Prabuddha, Buddha, Kāla. A dialogue in which Garuḍa questions Śiva. An old Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript is dated 924 CE (scholarly report). Its vidyāpāda (12 paṭalas: paśu, māyā, karma, pati, śaktipāta, dīkṣā, mantra, bhuvana, śivatattva, tantrāvatāra, mātṛkā, yantra) is an early statement of Siddhānta doctrine.

attribution.tradition: Mārkaṇḍeya tells Jaimini to go to the four wise birds (sons of Droṇa) in the Vindhya, who answer his questions (MkP 1-3; Matsya 53.25-26).
attribution.scholarly: One of the older Purāṇas, with little sectarian colouring; the Devī Māhātmya (chs. 81-93 in the Venkateshwara/Sansknet numbering, 78-90 in some others) is a separable later insertion.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

scholarly.text: core c. 3rd-6th c. CE; Devī Māhātmya c. 5th-6th c. CE

structure.description: c. 134-137 chapters in full editions (the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text has chs. 1-93); 9,000 verses by the traditional count

notes: Chs. 10-15: Sumati ('Jaḍa') on death, the road of Yama and the hells, and Vipaścit; 16-44: Dattātreya's birth and his teaching (through Madālasā's son Alarka) - yoga chs. 39-43; 45-80: creation, time, cosmography and the manvantaras; 81-93: Devī Māhātmya. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the MkP (chs. 1-93; Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81-93 in this numbering)
summary: A Purāṇa of dialogues: the birth, death and after-death journey of beings; the hells; Madālasā's teaching to her sons; Dattātreya's yoga for Alarka (posture, breath, dhāraṇā, obstacles, powers, Oṃ, the signs of death); creation, time and the fourteen manvantaras; and the Devī Māhātmya.

Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).

summary: The earliest surviving Śaiva tantra and No. 12 (Rudrabheda) of the 28 Siddhānta scriptures. It comprises five books — Niśvāsamukha, Mūlasūtra, Uttarasūtra, Nayasūtra, Guhyasūtra — teaching the fivefold hierarchy of religion (worldly, Vedic, spiritual, Atimārga, Mantramārga), early Śaiva initiation and ritual, doctrine and yoga. The Kāmika assigns it 8 upabheda(s): Niśvāsottara, Niśvāsa, Niśvāsamukhodaya, Niśvāsanayana, Niśvāsakārikā, Ghorasaṃjña, Yama, Guhya.

title: Nyāyabhāṣya

attribution.tradition: Vātsyāyana, also called Pakṣilasvāmin (so named by Vācaspati).
attribution.scholarly: Vātsyāyana; before Dignāga, who criticizes him.

summary: Vātsyāyana's commentary, the oldest extant on the Nyāya Sūtra. It explains that a means of knowledge is purposeful because it makes action successful, defines nyāya as the examination of things by the means of knowledge, presents ānvīkṣikī as the fourth science distinct from the Upaniṣadic science of the self, reads the five members as a convergence of all four means of knowledge, catalogues the forms of false knowledge, rejects eternal pleasure in liberation, describes Īśvara as a distinct self who assists human effort, and prescribes yama, niyama, yoga and contemplation of the unlovely against passion.

title: Nyāyakusumāñjali

structure.description: 5 stabakas of kārikās with Udayana's prose; verse numbering varies by edition

summary: Udayana's 'handful of flowers of reasoning' offered to the Lord: in five clusters (stabaka) of verses with his own prose, it answers five objections to Īśvara — that there is no supersensible means to the other world, that such means can work without Him, that there are proofs of His non-existence, that even if He exists He is not an authority, and that there is no proof of Him — and gives, in 5.1, the classic list of proofs. It presents reasoning about the Lord as a form of worship and opens with a passage on the names under which the schools worship Him.
notes: Commentaries include Vardhamāna's Prakāśa; verse numbers used in this unit are from memory and marked low.

summary: The root text of Nyāya. It opens by promising the highest good (niḥśreyasa) from knowledge of the truth of sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1), states the chain from false knowledge to liberation (1.1.2), defines the four means of knowledge, the twelve objects of knowledge beginning with the self, the five-membered demonstration, debate, pseudo-reasons, quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat (book 1); examines the means of knowledge (book 2), the self, body, senses, cognition and mind (book 3), faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation, the whole and atoms, rival views such as momentariness and idealism, and the yogic means to knowledge of truth (book 4); and lists the twenty-four futile rejoinders and twenty-two points of defeat (book 5).

title: Nyāyāmṛta

structure.description: 4 paricchedas

summary: Vyāsatīrtha's great polemic against Advaita, in four chapters that follow the four chapters of the Brahmasūtras: (1) the reality of the world — a refutation of the five Advaita definitions of falsity (mithyātva) and of the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness; (2) the Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite, attributeless meaning, and the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; (3) the means — against the Vivaraṇa view of hearing, reflection and meditation, the Lord is to be won by direct realization born of meditation; (4) liberation is not the mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated, from Brahmā and Rudra down, are graded. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it point by point.
notes: Four paricchedas, their opening sections and concluding sentences checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Padārthadharmasaṅgraha

summary: A vast Vaiṣṇava-leaning compendium: creation, tīrthas (Puṣkara and others), vratas (Ekādaśī, Kārttika, Māgha), the glory of the Bhāgavata and the Gītā, Rāma narratives, the worship of the name and of the śālagrāma and tulasī, and the guṇa-classification of the eighteen Purāṇas.

summary: A short Kaula-Trika dialogue: the Goddess asks how the Unsurpassed (anuttara) grants immediate Kaula perfection. Bhairava teaches the emanation of the letters as the tattvas (vv. 5-9), the Heart of Bhairava as the 'third Brahman' (10), the powers of reciting and remembering it (11-20), the tattvas from Kālāgni to Śiva (21-23), the universe resting in the Heart-seed as a banyan tree in its seed (24), initiation for one who knows this (25), and a worship procedure (26-33). It closes 'this is the Rudrayāmala' (35).

Its upabheda list includes arts and sciences (medicine, archery, music, dramaturgy).

title: Pṛthivī Sūkta (Atharvaveda 12.1)
summary: The sixty-three-verse hymn to the Earth: she is upheld by truth, great order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice; 'the Earth is mother, I am her son'; she bears peoples of many speeches and many dharmas; the digger asks that what he digs may grow again and that he not strike her vitals or heart.

title: Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90)
summary: The hymn of the cosmic Person: thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed, covering the earth and exceeding it by ten fingers; all this is Puruṣa, past and future; one quarter of him is all beings, three quarters the immortal in heaven; from him Virāj was born and from Virāj he; the gods sacrificed Puruṣa as the oblation, and from that sacrifice came the verses, chants, metres and formulas, the animals, the four varṇas from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, Indra and Agni from his mouth, wind from his breath, and the worlds; 'with the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; these were the first dharmas'.

attribution.tradition: seen by narayana-rsi; deity: Puruṣa (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Also Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 31.1–16 (with the six 'Uttaranārāyaṇa' verses 31.17–22), Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 19.6 and Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12 (last two from memory). Its sixteen verses are used for the sixteen-fold worship in later temple and domestic ritual.

title: Pūrvapañcikā
summary: Abhinavagupta's commentary on the Pūrvatantra (the Mālinīvijayottara), referred to in his other works; lost.

title: Puṣpasūtra
summary: A Sāmaveda treatise on how verses are transformed into chants: the modifications (vikāra), insertions of stobhas and the distribution of melodies over the verses.

attribution.tradition: ascribed to Gobhila or to Vararuci (reports differ)
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic sūtra of the Sāmavedins

notes: Authorship reports recalled from memory; to be checked.

title: Rājadharma (Rājadharmānuśāsanaparvan)

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara yuga, before the Kali yuga (traditionally reckoned from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: composed and expanded in stages, c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

structure.description: 128 chapters (CE 12.1–128), about 4,500 verse units

summary: Bhīṣma's instruction to Yudhiṣṭhira on the dharma of kings: the origin of kingship and of the science of punishment (daṇḍanīti), protection of subjects, counsel, taxation, war, and the duties of the varṇas and āśramas; preceded by the family's arguments persuading Yudhiṣṭhira not to renounce.

title: Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti)

scholarly.text: first half of the 11th c. CE (reign of Bhoja of Dhārā, c. 1010–1055)

summary: King Bhoja's concise vṛtti on the sūtras (not on the bhāṣya). It sets out the four samprajñāta samādhis as savitarka, savicāra, sānanda and sāsmita, calls those who rest content in bliss 'videhas' and those who rest in I-am-ness 'prakṛtilayas', and treats discernment of the supreme puruṣa as the grasper-coalescence (1.17); asamprajñāta is reached by rejecting every arising activity 'not this, not this' (1.18); devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to the supreme teacher without desire for fruit (1.23, 2.1).

title: Rājaśēkharavilāsa (Ṣaḍakṣaradēva)
summary: A seventeenth-century Kannada campū narrating a Śaiva devotional legend, a classic of later Vīraśaiva poetry.

title: Rājavārttika (Sāṃkhya)

attribution.tradition: unknown
attribution.scholarly: Lost work quoted by Vācaspati Miśra (Tattvakaumudī on SK 72) for the verses enumerating the sixty topics; author unknown.

summary: A lost Sāṃkhya work known from Vācaspati Miśra's quotation of its verses listing the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra (ten fundamental topics and the fifty).
notes: Quotation recalled from the Tattvakaumudī on SK 72 (not in the local partial text).

title: Rāma Gītā

attribution.tradition: Rāma's teaching to Lakṣmaṇa, 'churned from the ocean of the Upaniṣads' (AR Māhātmya), narrated by Śiva to Pārvatī
attribution.scholarly: part of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; a compact Advaita manual

scholarly.text: with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, c. 14th-15th c. CE

structure.description: one sarga of 62 verses

summary: After one's duties have purified the mind, one should approach a true guru: ignorance is the root of rebirth and only knowledge removes it, not action, so knowledge cannot be combined with ritual action; the meaning of 'that thou art' is grasped by partial implication; the self is distinct from the three bodies and three states; superimposition is explained; one meditates on the Self, dissolves the syllables of Oṃ into it, lives out prārabdha free of ego and merges in Rāma. Until all is seen as Rāma, one should worship him.

editions.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (Gita Press); Gītāsaṅgraha (Poona 1915)

title: Rāma Gītā (Tattvasārāyaṇa)

attribution.tradition: Rāma's teaching to Hanumān
attribution.scholarly: late; distinct from the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa's Rāma Gītā

summary: A longer Rāma Gītā (recalled as 18 chapters) in which Rāma teaches Hanumān Vedānta and yoga; distinct from the 62-verse Rāma Gītā of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.
notes: Recalled only; flagged for the hallucination sweep.

title: Rāma-hṛdaya
location_in_parent: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Bālakāṇḍa 1 (Sītā's teaching 1.1.31-43; Rāma's 1.1.44-52; named at 1.1.53)

attribution.tradition: Rāma's own teaching to Hanumān after the coronation, introduced by Sītā; Śiva calls it the essence of all Vedānta
attribution.scholarly: part of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa

scholarly.text: with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, c. 14th-15th c. CE

summary: Sītā tells Hanumān that Rāma is the non-dual Brahman and she the primal nature who does all the deeds attributed to him; Rāma then teaches the threefold consciousness (the whole, the consciousness delimited by the intellect, and its reflection) by the example of the threefold sky, and that the great sayings reveal the identity whose knowledge destroys ignorance, provided one has devotion.

title: Rāmarudrī
summary: Rāmarudra Bhaṭṭa's commentary on the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī (a gloss continuing the Dinakarī).

title: Rāmāyaṇa (of Vālmīki)

attribution.tradition: Composed by the sage Vālmīki after Nārada told him Rāma's story; the first śloka arose from his grief at a hunter's killing of one of a pair of krauñca birds (1.2.15–18); sung by Rāma's sons Kuśa and Lava.
attribution.scholarly: An oral-bardic work fixed in writing over centuries; the first and seventh books are widely held to be later additions; transmitted in northern and southern recensions.

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki in the Tretā yuga, in Rāma's own time

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE – 3rd c. CE, in stages; books 2–6 generally held older than books 1 and 7

structure.description: 7 books (kāṇḍas). The poem itself speaks of 24,000 ślokas in 500 sargas, six books and the Uttara (1.4.2, vulgate). The local southern vulgate text has Bāla 77, Ayodhyā 119, Araṇya 75, Kiṣkindhā 67, Sundara 68, Yuddha 128, Uttara 111 sargas. The Baroda critical edition (1960–75) constitutes a shorter text.

summary: The first poem (ādikāvya): the life of Rāma, prince of Ayodhyā — his exile in obedience to his father's word, the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa, the alliance with the monkeys and Hanumān, the war in Laṅkā, his righteous reign, and (in the last book) the banishment of Sītā. It presents Rāma as dharma embodied: truth to one's word, obedience to parents, fraternal loyalty, protection of those who seek refuge, and the king's duty to his subjects.

summary: Govindarāja's extensive Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary on the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa.

title: Rātri Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.127)
summary: Night as a goddess who looks out with many eyes, fills the wide space, drives away darkness with her light, and gives rest to villages, beasts and birds; she is asked to ward off wolf and thief.

attribution.tradition: seen by ratri-bharadvaji; deity: Rātri (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Seer given as Kuśika Saubhara or Rātri Bhāradvājī (checked in the local text's header). A separate Rātri Sūkta is recited with the Devī Māhātmya (reference only).

title: Rauravāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Brāhmaṇeśa, then Nandikeśa (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Rudrabheda no. 16 in the Kāmika's order; 6 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: Rauravāgama, ed. N. R. Bhatt, Institut Français d'Indologie (3 vols, 1961, 1972, 1988)

notes: Kiraṇa 10.17/10.25: Brahmaṇeśa → Nandikeśvara. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Raurava'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the ears (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 16 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Brāhmaṇeśa, then Nandikeśa. The Kāmika assigns it 6 upabheda(s): Kālaghna, Kalātīta, Raurava, Rauravottara, Mahākālamata, Aindra. The first volume of Bhatt's edition includes the Rauravasūtrasaṅgraha (src:rauravasutrasangraha).

title: Rauravasūtrasaṅgraha

title: Ṛbhu Gītā
location_in_parent: Śivarahasya, sixth part (aṃśa) (low confidence on the exact chapters)

attribution.tradition: Ṛbhu, a son of Brahmā and devotee of Śiva, teaches the non-dual truth he received from Śiva to his disciple Nidāgha
attribution.scholarly: part of the Śivarahasya, a large Śaiva 'itihāsa' of South Indian provenance; date uncertain

tradition.text: taught by Ṛbhu, son of Brahmā (mythic time)

structure.description: Sanskrit text of some two thousand verses in several dozen chapters (exact count not verified); a Tamil rendering (Ṛbhu Gītai) in 44 chapters exists

summary: Relentless statements that all is Brahman and that nothing else exists: the world, the jīva, mind, time, bondage and liberation are declared non-existent in the one consciousness; hearing and contemplating this teaching is itself presented as liberating, alongside Śaiva observances (sacred ash, rudrākṣa, worship of Śiva).
notes: The same teacher-disciple pair (Ṛbhu and Nidāgha) appears in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15-16 (verified in the local e-text). Ramana Maharshi recommended the Ṛbhu Gītā and it was read in his presence (recent reception). Chapter structure and verse counts are not verified here.

title: Ṛgarthadīpikā (Veṅkaṭamādhava)
summary: A concise commentary on the whole Ṛgveda by Veṅkaṭamādhava, giving brief glosses and the sense of each verse.

title: Ṛgarthoddhāra
summary: Śrīnivāsa Tīrtha's exposition of the meaning of the Ṛgveda hymns covered by Madhva's Ṛgbhāṣya.
notes: Title and author as in the raw_etexts file names.

title: Ṛgbhāṣya (Madhva)

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

structure.description: Ṛgveda 1.1–1.40

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a verse commentary on the first forty hymns of the Ṛgveda (1.1–1.40), opening with the claim that Nārāyaṇa alone is the meaning of all the Vedas, all śāstras and all words, and explaining names such as Agni as primarily designating Janārdana.
notes: Coverage of sūktas 1–40 and the opening verses checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.
alt_summary: Madhva's commentary on the first forty hymns of the Ṛgveda, which reads the hymns as ultimately praising Viṣṇu, the one denoted by all names, and holds that the mantras carry several levels of meaning.
alt_notes: Commented on by Jayatīrtha and Rāghavendra (reference from memory). The 'three meanings' doctrine is recalled with moderate confidence.

title: Ṛgbhāṣya-ṭīkā (Jayatīrtha)
summary: Jayatīrtha's commentary on Madhva's Ṛgbhāṣya, relating the words of the hymns to the bhāṣya's glosses.
notes: Title and author checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā
summary: The oldest Vedic collection: hymns (sūktas) of praise and invocation to Agni, Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, the Aśvins, Uṣas, Rudra, Viṣṇu and others, recited by the hotṛ priest. Beside the liturgy it contains speculative hymns on the One (1.164, 10.129, 10.121, 10.90, 10.125), on speech, on the self and on death and the fathers (10.14–18).

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; each hymn's seer (ṛṣi), deity and metre are recorded by the Anukramaṇīs
attribution.scholarly: composed by priestly poet families over several centuries and redacted into the Śākala recension

tradition.text: beginningless; the hymns were 'seen' by the ṛṣis and handed down (Nirukta 1.20)

scholarly.text: c. 1500–1000 BCE; family books (2–7) earliest, books 1 and 10 latest

structure.description: 10 maṇḍalas; 1,028 sūktas counting the 11 Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59); c. 10,550 verses (counts differ slightly). Books 2–7 are the family books: 2 Gṛtsamada, 3 Viśvāmitra, 4 Vāmadeva, 5 Atri, 6 Bharadvāja, 7 Vasiṣṭha; book 8 chiefly the Kāṇvas (and Āṅgirasas); book 9 the hymns to Soma Pavamāna gathered from all families; books 1 and 10 are collections of many seers and are regarded as later. A second division into 8 aṣṭakas × 8 adhyāyas (64 adhyāyas) and vargas is used for recitation.

title: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Ṛgveda (Vedārthaprakāśa)
summary: The complete classical commentary on the Ṛgveda, produced at Vijayanagara under Sāyaṇa's direction: it glosses every word, explains each hymn chiefly by its use in the sacrifice (yajña), draws on Yāska, the Brāhmaṇas and earlier commentators, and in its introduction defines the Veda and defends its authority. Most traditional and modern readings of the Ṛgveda start from it.

attribution.tradition: Sāyaṇa (the commentaries are also called 'Mādhavīya', after his brother Mādhava)
attribution.scholarly: composed by Sāyaṇa with collaborators, 14th century

title: Skandasvāmin's commentary on the Ṛgveda
summary: An early surviving Ṛgveda commentary, covering part of the Saṃhitā, which explains words through Yāska's etymologies and the ritual.
notes: Tradition reports that Skandasvāmin worked with Nārāyaṇa and Udgītha on the whole Ṛgveda; only parts survive (low confidence).

title: The funeral hymns (Ṛgveda 10.14–18)
summary: The hymns for the dead: homage to Yama, first of mortals to find the path to the fathers (10.14); invocation of the fathers (10.15); the cremation fire asked not to consume the body utterly but to carry the dead, cooked, to the fathers, eye to the sun, breath to the wind (10.16); Pūṣan as guide on the far paths (10.17); death sent away on its own path, the living set apart by a boundary, the widow bidden to rise to the world of the living, and the bones laid in mother earth (10.18).

attribution.tradition: seen by yama-vaivasvata (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Seers per the Anukramaṇī: 10.14 Yama Vaivasvata; 10.15 Śaṅkha Yāmāyana; 10.16 Damana Yāmāyana; 10.17 Devaśravas Yāmāyana; 10.18 Saṅkusuka Yāmāyana (checked in the local text).

title: Ṛgveda Khilāni (the supplementary hymns)
summary: A collection of supplementary hymns (khila) transmitted alongside the Śākala Saṃhitā — most fully in a Kashmiri manuscript — including the Śrī Sūkta, the Medhā Sūkta, the Śivasaṅkalpa verses and other hymns used in later worship.

attribution.tradition: part of the revealed hymns, not counted in the Saṃhitā
attribution.scholarly: later additions from the late Vedic period onward

structure.description: about 5 adhyāyas of khila hymns in the Kashmiri recension (as edited by Scheftelowitz, 1906)

notes: Division and contents recalled from memory; the Kashmiri manuscript edition (Scheftelowitz 1906) to be confirmed.

title: Ṛgveda Padapāṭha
summary: The word-by-word recitation of the Ṛgveda, ascribed to Śākalya, which undoes the euphonic combinations (sandhi) and marks compound members, so that every word and accent of the continuous text is fixed; it is the basis of the krama and other interwoven recitations and the oldest witness to how the tradition understood each word.

attribution.tradition: Śākalya
attribution.scholarly: the Padapāṭha is very old (pre-Pāṇinian); Śākalya is cited by Yāska and Pāṇini

scholarly.text: before Yāska and Pāṇini (c. 7th–5th c. BCE)

structure.description: follows the Saṃhitā hymn by hymn; omits a few verses it treats as not part of the Saṃhitā proper (e.g. 10.121.10 and the Vālakhilya hymns, as usually reported)

notes: The omission of 10.121.10 and of the Vālakhilya hymns from the Padapāṭha is recalled from secondary literature — confidence moderate.

title: Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya
summary: The Śākala school's treatise on the phonetics of the Ṛgveda: sounds, accents, the rules for joining the words of the Padapāṭha into the continuous text, and the krama recitation.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic phonetic treatise of the Śākala school

title: Ṛgvedādibhāṣyabhūmikā (Dayānanda Sarasvatī)
summary: Dayānanda Sarasvatī's introduction to his Veda commentaries: the four Saṃhitās alone are the eternal revelation of one God; the names Agni, Indra and the rest denote that one God; the Vedas contain no history of persons; their knowledge is open to all.
notes: Recent (post-1800). Dates recalled with moderate confidence.

title: Ṛgvidhāna
summary: A manual on the uses (vidhāna) of Ṛgveda hymns and verses for purification, expiation, healing and the fulfilment of wishes by recitation (japa) and oblation, ascribed to Śaunaka.

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina)
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of a hundred paths', the great Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda. It explains the whole Śrauta ritual — new- and full-moon, fire establishment, Agnihotra, ancestral offering, seasonal rites, Soma, royal consecration, the fire-altar (Agnicayana, books 6–10, with its 'secret' in book 10), horse, human and all-sacrifice, the funeral mound, the Pravargya — and teaches the sacrifice as the cosmic Person and year: Prajāpati fell apart after emitting creatures and is rebuilt in the altar. It records the teaching of Śāṇḍilya (10.6.3), the debates of Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court, the debts, the five great sacrifices, upanayana, Vedic self-study, the flood, and ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (14.4–9).

title: Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram, Rudrādhyāya)

Its eighth section contains 'namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca', the source the Śaiva traditions give for the five-syllable formula.
notes: Used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra; recited in the tradition as Rudra-japa (Ekādaśa-, Laghu-, Mahā-, Atirudra) and in Śaiva worship. The Jābāla Upaniṣad names śatarudrīya recitation as a means to immortality (reference only).

title: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta's encyclopaedic exposition of the Trika on the basis of the Mālinīvijayottara, integrating Kaula and Krama. After defining bondage as ignorance and knowledge as the sole cause of liberation (1.22-23), it orders all Śaiva practice by the four means (chs. 2-5), sets out time, space, the tattvas and the paths of manifestation (6-12), the descent of grace (13), the whole ritual of initiation, consecration, funerary and daily rites (14-28), the secret Kula ritual (29), mantra, maṇḍala and mudrā (30-32), and ends with unification, the harmony of the scriptures, the lineage and the author's account of himself (33-37).

structure.description: 37 āhnikas (chapters), c. 5,800 verses; chapter topics per Abhinavagupta's own table of contents (TĀ 1.278-329) and colophons: 1 vijñānabheda (the kinds of knowledge; knowledge as the cause of liberation; table of contents); 2 anupāya (the means-less); 3 śāmbhavopāya (the reflection of the universe in consciousness; the letters); 4 śāktopāya (purification of thought, sattarka, the wheel of consciousness, the twelve Kālīs, critique of rules); 5 āṇavopāya (meditation, uccāra of prāṇa, the seven ānandas, the five signs, karaṇa, varṇa); 6 kālopāya / kālatattva (time in the breath and its cycles); 7 cakrodaya (the arising of the wheels; mantra and breath counts); 8 deśādhvan (the path of space: the worlds); 9 tattvādhvan (the path of the tattvas); 10 tattvabheda (divisions of the tattvas; the states and the seven pramātṛs); 11 kalādhvan (the path of the kalās; letters and mantras); 12 adhvopayoga (use of the paths); 13 śaktipāta (the descent of power; its grades); 14 dīkṣopakrama (preliminaries of initiation; removal of concealment); 15 samayadīkṣā (initiation into the samaya; the samaya rules); 16 prameya (the putraka initiation and the knowables purified); 17 vikṣipta/extended initiation (cord, purification of the tattvas, burning the bonds); 18 saṅkṣiptadīkṣā (abbreviated initiation); 19 sadyaḥsamutkrānti (initiation bringing immediate departure from the body); 20 tulādīkṣā (initiation by the balance); 21 parokṣadīkṣā (initiation of the absent and the dead); 22 liṅgoddhāra (removal of a prior sectarian mark); 23 abhiṣeka (consecration as teacher or adept); 24 antyeṣṭi (final rites); 25 śrāddha (rites for the dead); 26 sthaṇḍilapūjā (daily worship on a ritual ground; the remaining life of the initiate); 27 liṅgārcā (worship of the liṅga); 28 parva-pavitraka etc. (occasional rites; the gathering of yoginīs; rites for the guru); 29 rahasyavidhi (the secret Kula ritual); 30 mantra (the mantras); 31 maṇḍala; 32 mudrā; 33 ekīkāra (unification of the paths); 34 svarūpapraveśa (entry into one's own nature); 35 śāstrasammelana (the harmony of the scriptures); 36 āyātikrama (the descent of the scripture through the lineage); 37 upādeyabhāva (why this scripture is to be accepted; the author's account of himself)

summary: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya's 'wish-gem of truth', the founding text of Navya-Nyāya, in four books (khaṇḍa) on perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony. They teach devotion to Śiva as the liṅga, the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), the triad of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama, work as worship (kāyaka) and giving (dāsōha), and criticize caste, pollution rules, temple and Vedic ritualism and outward show in favour of lived experience (anubhava).

summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika in ten books. It announces the explanation of dharma — that from which prosperity and the highest good result — and grounds the Veda's authority; lists the nine substances, the qualities and the five motions and defines substance, quality and motion; treats being, universals and particulars, the elements, time, space, the self (with its marks and plurality) and the atomic mind; atoms and perception; motions caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa); yoga and liberation; ethics of giving, food and ritual observances; inherence; absence; perception, inference and memory; and the seers' knowledge.

title: Vijñānabhairava
summary: A dialogue in which the Goddess (Bhairavī) asks Bhairava about his true nature; he rejects every form 'with parts' (the ninefold, the mass of sounds, the three-headed, nāda-bindu...) as a device for the confused (vv. 7-13), describes the supreme state as indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess (14-21), and in answer to her request for means (22-23) teaches 112 contemplations (dhāraṇā) of the 'waveless state' (24-138; counted at 139). It then redefines japa, meditation, worship, oblation, sacrifice and bathing as inner acts (144-153), teaches the natural 'haṃsa' repetition of the breath (154-156), enjoins secrecy (157-160), and closes with the Goddess embracing Śiva, having grasped 'the essence of the Rudrayāmala' (161-163).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava to Bhairavī; claims to be the essence of the Rudrayāmala and of the Trika (vv. 1, 161-162).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous. The claimed Rudrayāmala origin cannot be verified: the early Rudrayāmala is lost, and the extant Rudrayāmala (Uttaratantra) is a different and later text. Cited by Kṣemarāja, who began a commentary on it.

title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)

attribution.tradition: By Vyāsa, identified with Veda-Vyāsa and with Bādarāyaṇa (Vijñānabhikṣu, Yogavārttika intro. and 1.1; Nārāyaṇatīrtha, Sūtrārthabodhinī intro.).
attribution.scholarly: The author's identity is unknown; Maas (following Bronkhorst and others) holds that sūtra and bhāṣya are one work by Patañjali; older scholarship placed the bhāṣya well after the sūtras. The bhāṣya cites 'Patañjali' by name once (3.44), a point used in this debate.

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if one work with the sūtras (Maas); older estimates placed it later (6th–8th c.)

structure.description: running prose commentary on all 195 sūtras, headed by a maṅgala verse to the lord of serpents; each pāda closes 'iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre ... vyāsabhāṣye'

summary: The oldest and authoritative commentary. It defines yoga as samādhi and names the five levels of mind (1.1); analyzes the vṛttis, the kleśas and their states (with a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state), karma and its fruition; gives the fourfold scheme modelled on medicine (2.15) and the sevenfold final insight (2.27); lists seated postures (2.46); explains saṃyama and the powers, the four kinds of yogin and the invitation of the celestials (3.51), and a detailed cosmology (3.26); and argues against Buddhist views of a momentary mind and of objects as mind-only (1.32, 4.14–24).

editions.name: Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47 (ed. K. Ś. Āgāśe, Pune 1904); GRETIL e-text
Pātañjaladarśana with Vyāsa's bhāṣya and Vijñānabhikṣu's Yogavārttika, ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (Calcutta); e-Bhāratī Sampat e-text

title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali

attribution.tradition: Composed by Patañjali as a re-teaching (anuśāsana, 1.1) of the yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha (Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa on 1.1); Patañjali is regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the lord of serpents, and identified with the grammarian of the Mahābhāṣya.
attribution.scholarly: Most scholars doubt that the Yoga author is the grammarian (c. 2nd c. BCE). Philipp A. Maas argues, following earlier arguments by J. Bronkhorst, that sūtras and bhāṣya form one work — the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, as the colophons ('pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre') call it — by one author, c. 325–425 CE; others treat the sūtras as older than the bhāṣya.

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (Patañjali as an incarnation of Śeṣa)

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE together with the bhāṣya (Maas); earlier proposals range from the 2nd c. BCE to the 5th c. CE

structure.description: 4 pādas: Samādhi (51 sūtras), Sādhana (55), Vibhūti (55), Kaivalya (34) = 195 sūtras in the Vyāsa-based vulgate (Ānandāśrama ed., and every local commentary e-text). Some editions count 196 by treating 'etena śabdādy antardhānam uktam' — part of the bhāṣya on 3.21 in the Ānandāśrama ed. — as a separate sūtra 3.22, shifting the later numbers of pāda 3 by one. This unit uses the 195-sūtra numbering.

summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana. It defines yoga as the stilling of the activities of the mind (1.2); teaches practice and dispassion, devotion to Īśvara and Oṃ, the obstacles and their remedies, the samāpattis and the kinds of samādhi (pāda 1); kriyā-yoga, the five afflictions, karma, the seer and the seen, and the first five of the eight limbs (pāda 2); concentration, meditation, samādhi, saṃyama, the transformations of mind and the powers with their warnings (pāda 3); and the sources of powers, karma and latent tendencies, the reality of objects, the non-self-luminosity of mind, the cloud of dharma and kaivalya (pāda 4).

Ph. A. Maas, Samādhipāda: das erste Kapitel des Pātañjalayogaśāstra zum ersten Mal kritisch ediert (Aachen 2006)

title: Pātañjalayogaśāstravivaraṇa (Yogasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇa)

attribution.tradition: Colophons ascribe it to Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, pupil of Govinda Bhagavatpāda.
attribution.scholarly: Disputed. P. Hacker and T. Leggett argued that it is an early work of the Advaita teacher Śaṅkara; T. S. Rukmani and others doubt the ascription and date it later; K. Harimoto critically edited the section on YS 1.23–28.

scholarly.text: uncertain: c. 8th c. CE if by Śaṅkara; later dates proposed

summary: A sub-commentary on Vyāsa's bhāṣya, first printed in 1952 (Madras Government Oriental Series), notable for its extended reasoning about Īśvara (1.23–28) and for the controversy over its ascription to Śaṅkara.

title: Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

attribution.tradition: composed by Vālmīki, author of the Rāmāyaṇa, and told to Bharadvāja: the dialogue in which Vasiṣṭha teaches Rāma, with Viśvāmitra present, at Daśaratha's court
attribution.scholarly: the vulgate is a Vedāntic revision of the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya (src:moksopaya), an anonymous 10th-c. philosophical poem; its non-dualism is close to but not identical with Śaṅkara's Advaita and shares vocabulary with Kashmiri Śaiva and Buddhist idealist thought

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki; the teaching given by Vasiṣṭha to the young Rāma in the Tretā age

scholarly.text: the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya c. 10th c. CE (Slaje, c. 950); the Vedānta-oriented Yoga Vāsiṣṭha vulgate is a later revision (c. 11th-14th c.); older proposals ranged from the 6th to the 13th c.

structure.description: 6 prakaraṇas: Vairāgya (dispassion, 33 sargas), Mumukṣu-vyavahāra (conduct of the seeker, 20), Utpatti (origination, 122), Sthiti (persistence, 62), Upaśama (quiescence, 93), Nirvāṇa (liberation, pūrvārdha 128 + uttarārdha 216). The text names itself Mokṣopāya and claims 32,000 verses (2.17.6); the printed vulgate has roughly 27,000-29,000

summary: Vasiṣṭha teaches the despondent young Rāma that the world is a projection of mind within the one consciousness (cit), arising like a dream; that human effort (pauruṣa) guided by scripture and the good overrides fate, which is only past effort; that liberation comes by inquiry (vicāra) with the four gatekeepers (peace, inquiry, contentment, holy company), by the weakening of latent tendencies (vāsanā) and the stilling of mind and breath, through seven stages of knowledge to liberation while living. The teaching is carried by dozens of stories (Līlā, Karkaṭī, Lavaṇa, Śukra, Dāśūra, Prahlāda, Bali, Gādhi, Uddālaka, Suraghu, Vītahavya, Bhuśuṇḍa, Cūḍālā and Śikhidhvaja, the stone and others).

editions.name: Yogavāsiṣṭha with Ānandabodhendra's Tātparyaprakāśa (Nirṇaya Sāgara, Bombay 1911/1918)
Vihari-Lala Mitra, The Yoga-vasishtha-maharamayana (1891-99)

notes: Book-level refs 1-5 in U06 teachings are checked against the Mokṣopāya critical edition, whose sarga numbering agrees with the vulgate for the passages used (e.g. the seven stages at 3.118, the gatekeepers at 2.11.59); Book 4 of the vulgate begins c. 18 sargas earlier than the MU's Book 4, and the vulgate splits Book 6 in two halves, so Book 4 and 6 teachings are anchored on src:moksopaya.

title: Yogadīpikā (Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya)

structure.description: 10 paṭalas

summary: A manual in ten paṭalas by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya on yoga as the Dvaita tradition understands it: yoga is the supreme worship of Hari with devotion through prescribed action; one remembers Hari as the real agent within one's limbs; it describes the training of a devotee, study and reflection on Madhva's works, initiation by the ācārya, worship with mantra and nyāsa, contemplation of oneself as the reflection (pratibimba) of Nārāyaṇa in the heart, a graded list of disciplines crowned by hearing, reflection, meditation, samādhi and bhakti, and the presence of Hari in both the worshipper and the image.
notes: Author named in the opening and closing colophons of the raw_etexts copy; verse references checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Yogajāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Sudhā, then Bhasma, then Vibhu (Kiraṇa: Prabhu) (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Śivabheda no. 2 in the Kāmika's order; 5 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: e-text from a manuscript of M.K.S. Bhattar, Madurai (Muktabodha M00250); IFP MS 39691

notes: Kiraṇa 10.4/10.7: Sudhā → Bhasma → Prabhu. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Yogaja'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the ankles (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 2 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Śivabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Sudhā, then Bhasma, then Vibhu (Kiraṇa: Prabhu). The Kāmika assigns it 5 upabheda(s): Vīṇāśikhottara, Tāra, Santa, Santati, Ātmayoga. Transmitted in South Indian manuscripts; mainly ritual (kriyā) content.

title: Yogamaṇiprabhā

attribution.tradition: Colophon: by Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, paramahaṃsa pupil of Govindānanda; each pāda is called part of the 'sāṅkhyapravacana' and of the Yogamaṇiprabhā.

scholarly.text: late 16th – 17th c. CE (inferred from his teacher Govindānanda)

summary: A vṛtti that follows the bhāṣya (bhāṣyānugā). On 1.1 it explains 'anuśāsana': although the śāstra was made by Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, considering it extensive, begins a śāstra that follows it.

title: Yōgāṅga Trividhi
summary: A short poem in tripadi metre ascribed to Akka Mahādēvi on yoga and the path to the liṅga.

title: Yogasārasaṅgraha

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's digest of the doctrine of the Yoga Sūtras as he expounds it in the Yogavārttika.
notes: Structure and contents not recalled in detail (gap).

title: Yogasiddhāntacandrikā
summary: Nārāyaṇatīrtha's extensive vṛtti. Its opening verses give the transmission (Pitāmaha taught yoga; Śeṣa in the sūtras; Vyāsa in the bhāṣya; Vācaspati Miśra and Vijñānabhikṣu clarified the bhāṣya) and argue that Vyāsa's Brahma Sūtras refuted pradhāna's independence, not yoga as meditative cultivation; the introduction treats deep contemplation (nididhyāsana) as samādhi, 'also called rājayoga', and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.

title: Yogasudhākara
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras ('the speech of the lord of serpents') by Sadāśiva Brahmendra, composed, as its closing verses say, by the grace of the teacher and offered at the teacher's feet.

title: Yogasūtradīpikā (Pradīpikā) of Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: A commentary 'for the easy understanding of the slow-witted' by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, who says it condenses the meaning examined in the bhāṣya and 'by my teacher himself in the Vārttika' (Vijñānabhikṣu).

title: Yogasūtravṛtti of Nāgeśa (Nāgojī) Bhaṭṭa
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras by the grammarian Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa. On 1.1 it says the śāstra expounds in detail the yoga taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and others; on 1.2 it glosses citta as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and nirodha as a special, supersensible effort that dissolves the activities.
notes: Nāgeśa is reported to have written a longer and a shorter vṛtti (Bṛhatī, Laghvī) — which one the local raw_etexts file contains is not verified.

title: Yogavallī
summary: A modern Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Sūtras. Its introduction surveys the darśanas, gives the count of 195 sūtras (51, 55, 55, 34), notes that some manuscripts mark the end of the work after pāda 3, cites the verse from Bhoja's vṛtti on Patañjali's three kinds of purification, and compares the Vivaraṇa, Tattvavaiśāradī and Yogavārttika on particular sūtras.
notes: Only the Samādhipāda is in the local raw_etexts file; author and date not identified (gap).

title: Yogavārttika

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's extensive sub-commentary on the bhāṣya. It calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda spoken by Vedavyāsa' and holds Sāṃkhya and the other darśanas to be contained in it like rivers in the ocean (intro.); cites the Yoga-Yājñavalkya for Hiraṇyagarbha as first teacher (1.1); argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi against a single-reflection view (1.7); gives its own account of the four samprajñāta samādhis (1.17); and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (1.51).

title: Yuktidīpikā

attribution.tradition: A colophon in the edition names Vācaspati Miśra ('kṛtir iyaṃ śrīvācaspatimiśrāṇām').
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; the colophon ascription to Vācaspati Miśra is not accepted.

structure.description: introductory verses and a commentary on the SK in four prakaraṇas and eleven āhnikas

summary: The most extensive old commentary on the SK. It defends Sāṃkhya against rival schools, preserves the divergent views of earlier Sāṃkhya teachers (Vārṣagaṇya, Vindhyavāsin, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Paurika, the Sāṃkhya teacher Patañjali), enumerates the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra and gives a list of teachers between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa.

title: Yuktimallikā

tradition.text: the tradition gives Vādirāja a life of 120 years (1480–1600)

summary: Vādirāja Tīrtha's major polemical verse treatise defending Dvaita doctrine — Viṣṇu's fullness of qualities, difference, the reality of the world and the nature of liberation — against Advaita.
notes: Its division into sections called 'saurabhas' is recalled at low confidence.
